name: HIIT
lead: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) alternates short, near-maximal bursts of exercise with brief recovery periods, usually in sessions under 30 minutes.[7] A related form, sprint interval training, uses all-out efforts.[2][7] It is promoted in fitness and looksmaxxing circles as a time-efficient way to lose fat and improve conditioning.

Meta-analyses find that HIIT improves cardiorespiratory fitness and several cardiometabolic markers, with body-composition changes that are modest and generally similar to moderate continuous training when compared in overweight adults.[3][4][7]

paras: Work intervals are commonly 20 to 45 seconds and rarely exceed 75 seconds, separated by recovery periods.[7] Researchers distinguish HIIT (near-maximal efforts) from sprint interval training (supramaximal efforts), both of which produce adaptations typical of moderate continuous training such as increased aerobic capacity.[2]

In the 1970s coach Peter Coe had Sebastian Coe run repeated fast 200 m efforts with short recovery. In 1996 Izumi Tabata and colleagues reported that four minutes a day of very intense cycling intervals matched the aerobic gains of about an hour of steady training in speed skaters. Martin Gibala's group published interval protocols in 2010 and 2011, and a 2012 proposal by Niels Vollaard suggested a ten-minute routine with two 20-second sprints.[7]

A meta-analysis in people with lifestyle-related cardiometabolic disease examined HIIT against moderate continuous training for fitness and safety.[1] A 65-study review of intervention trials assessed cardiometabolic outcomes in adults.[3] A meta-analysis of HIIT and glucose regulation reported effects on insulin resistance.[5] A review asked whether HIIT is a time-efficient strategy to improve health and fitness.[6]

For body composition, a systematic review in overweight and obese adults compared HIIT with moderate continuous training.[4] Encyclopedic summaries report modest reductions in subcutaneous fat and say HIIT may be less effective than longer sessions for obesity or for building muscle and bone mass.[7]

The American College of Sports Medicine advises consulting a doctor first, especially with coronary heart disease history.[7] Reported risks include injury, acute stress responses such as elevated cortisol and poorer sleep, and, with sustained overload, possible reductions in testosterone, thyroid function and bone density.[7]

Dozens of randomised trials and several meta-analyses exist. They show improved fitness and cardiometabolic markers and, for fat loss, modest effects broadly comparable to moderate continuous training.[1][3][4][5] A trial in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has also examined HIIT.[6]

timeline.event: Tabata and colleagues publish their interval protocol in speed skaters.[7]
Gibala's McMaster group publishes 60-second interval protocol.[7]
Major meta-analysis in cardiometabolic disease published.[1]

lore.intro: HIIT is commonly presented in fitness communities as a fat-loss tool; the claims below reflect that general framing rather than specific threads.

claims.claim: HIIT burns fat faster than steady cardio.
claims.believers: Proponents say short intense efforts burn more per minute and raise post-exercise metabolism.
claims.experts: A meta-analysis in overweight adults compared the two and reviews report modest, broadly similar body-composition effects.[4][7]

claims.claim: A few minutes is enough to improve fitness.
claims.believers: Advocates cite protocols with brief sprint bouts.
claims.experts: Research reports improved cardiorespiratory fitness with low time commitments, though protocols vary.[6][7]

card.summary: Short all-out interval workouts; well supported for fitness, with modest fat-loss effects similar to steady cardio.
card.note: Check with a doctor first if you have heart disease, per ACSM.

quick.overview:
HIIT is exercise in hard bursts separated by short recoveries, usually finishing within half an hour.

Research shows clear gains in fitness and metabolic markers; fat-loss effects are modest.
quick.mechanism: Near-maximal efforts drive adaptations such as greater aerobic capacity, similar to those from longer moderate training.
quick.risks: Injury, soreness and fatigue are reported; sustained overload may disturb hormones and sleep, and people with heart conditions are advised to seek medical clearance.
